newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Vranitzky says time to go after decade.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Vranitzky says time to go after decade.

text.p: Austrian Chancellor Franz Vranitzky, acclaimed for leading his country into the European Union and apologising to Jews for Austria's part in the Nazi Holocaust, resigned after nearly 11 years in power.

Vranitzky, Europe's second longest-serving leader after German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, on Saturday announced he was stepping down and named Finance Minister Viktor Klima as his successor as chancellor and Social Democratic Party leader.

The soft-spoken chancellor did much during his term of office to restore Austria's image abroad after the controversial presidency of Kurt Waldheim, who was criticised for trying to obscure his past in Hitler's Wehrmacht.

At home, while Vranitzky's won respect as a cool-headed captain of a sometimes turbulent coalition government, his party's popularity waned over the past decade and lost votes largely to the far right led by Joerg Haider.

Vranitzky, 59, said his going had nothing to do with his party's abysmal results in last October's European elections nor with any strife within his coalition with the conservative People's Party led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel.
He said it was just time to go.
"I thought that after so many years it would be a wise decision to transfer responsibility to younger people in the party," he told reporters after announcing his resignation.

Social Democrat parliamentary speaker Heinz Fischer said Vranitzky was leaving because of no political crisis or scandal, nor was he being pushed: "He just believed it was better for the country and this point in time was optimal."
Schuessel, who is also vice-chancellor, appeared taken aback by the announcement and gave no appraisal, good or bad, of his partner's 10 years in power.
"He did not inform us ahead of time as would have been customary," a clearly irritated Schuessel said.
The two parties, which have dominated Austrian politics since 1945, have been at each other's throats over the past two years in a struggle of power and one-upmanship.

The coalition broke down in October 1995 in a row over the budget deficit and nearly collapsed again last week in a battle over the privatisation of the country's second biggest bank, Creditanstalt-Bankverein.
Nationalist Freedom Party leader Haider knew when to hit below the belt by saying Vranitzky had ruined the Social Democrats and the time had come for him to go.
"My prophecy that I would still be working for Austria while he would be long gone has come true," said Haider, who also predicts he will be chancellor by the turn of the century.
Vranitzky's political career has been shadowed by that of Haider. Both took over the leadership of their parties within months of each other in 1986.

The Euro-sceptic Freedom Party, once dismissed by Vranitzky as just a protest party, came within 60,000 votes of the once-mighty Social Democrats in the Euro-poll, capturing a swathe of their traditional working-class support.
President Thomas Klestil, who formally accepted Vranitzky's resignation, was more statesman-like, praising the chancellor for leading Austria through difficult years.
The dapper Klima, 49, has yet to make any public statement, though was apparently reluctant to be persuaded to become Austria's eighth chancellor since 1945.
"I did have a different plan for my life, but I guess I'm going to do it," he told Austrian television briefly on his mobile telephone before the line broke up.

Outside Austria, Vranitzky may be best remembered for his landmark official visit to Israel in 1993 when he said Austria, too, had been responsible for the horrors committed by Hitler's Nazi regime. He told the Austrian parliament in a memorable speech two years earlier that Austria had to apologise for what happened during "those dark years".
One of his most triumphant moments came in June 1994 when more than two-thirds of the Austrian electorate voted in a referendum to join the European Union.
